sweep_summary: Two title hits, neither readable online. (1) Borges 2009, Leiden MA thesis 'Some prosodic features of Soninke of Gambia', 121 pp.: print only (Leiden UB Closed Stack 3, 8553 A 42; OCLC 778344413; not in the Leiden student-theses repository, no Google Books preview). Relevance unclear from the title, but it is the only first-hand prosodic study of a western (Gambian) variety, and Creissels (2015 p.2, 2016 pp.5/27-28) says western varieties may have substantially different prosodic systems and Bakel may be losing tone — so high acquisition priority as a possible variety-level refinement. (2) Rialland 1991, Linguistique Africaine 7: 117-124, her reply to Creissels 1991 'Remarques sur le système tonal du soninké' defending Rialland 1990 'Le système prosodique du soninké' (HAL metadata only, keyword Tonology): a tonological debate on Kaédi Soninke, not a stress description; print only, low priority. Nothing found contradicts the 'tonal' coding. New first-hand text read: Creissels 2015 CALL paper (author's site) states 'Kingi Soninke has two contrastive level tones, H and L' with no stress/accent — confirms, does not supersede Creissels 2016. findings rest on Glottolog, HAL, Crossref, Leiden Primo, LPP, Google Books and Creissels' site downloads.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog and Creissels 2015 code Soninke as a tone language with contrastive H vs. L on every syllable (lexical minimal pairs) and mention no stress. Platiel instead holds that the tonal system has lost its distinctive character (only traces survive) and that the language has an intensity accent whose placement is conditioned by syllable structure (heavy CVV or pre-geminate syllable), with lexically variable placement in CVCV words. Both the type (accent vs. contrastive tone) and the existence of word stress differ. Her data come from her own materials and the DNAFLA Soninke-French lexicon (Mali, 1979; note 2 p. 106), i.e. Malian Soninke; note 3 (p. 106) records that Diagana's 1980 Paris…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Platiel treats Soninke as a former two-register tone language whose tonal oppositions have lost most of their distinctive value, combined with an intensity accent (stress); a word carries a single accent except in compounds (p. 95). Its place is fixed by syllable structure: a word with a long vowel (CVVCV) is always stressed on that first, heavy syllable, with low register; a word with a geminate (CVCCV) is always stressed on the syllable before the geminate, i.e. the first, with high register (p. 80: 'CCV : accent d'intensité de registre haut frappant, non pas cette syllabe mais celle qui la précède'); CVCV words show only tendencies, splitting into three lexical groups (stress on the 1st syllable, on the 2nd, or no stress, all high register) with only exceptional minimal pairs; CVNCV words never stress the first syllable and show at most a weak high-register stress on the second in slow careful speech. Tri- and quadrisyllables follow the same rules according to where CVV or CC sits (p. 99).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: 'à l'exception des mots composés, un mot ne peut porter qu'un seul accent d'intensité' (p. 95); compounds may carry more than one.
new_statements.exceptions: CVCV words: three lexical groups differing in accent place (1st syllable, 2nd syllable, none), with rare minimal pairs and many doublets (p. 99); CVNCV words: no accent on the first syllable, only a very weak one on the second (pp. 99-100); nine monosyllabic grammatical words and about 30 Arabic loans with initial a-/al- fall outside the syllable canon (pp. 80-81). Platiel adds that the distinctive use of tonal and accentual oppositions 'n'est maintenant utilisé que très exceptionnellement' (p. 105).

Adds that an earlier first-hand description (O. Diagana 1980, 1984, Kaédi, Mauritania; not opened) analysed the language as tone plus accent. new_statements.rule_in_words: An autosegmental analysis of noun-phrase tone: Soninke is a two-tone (H, B=L) language; noun bases carry one of four base tonal schemes (B, BH, HB, H), number morphemes are H, determiners B, BHB or H, and surface melodies follow from tone-to-nucleus association within tonal domains defined by the determiner. Nothing is said about stress or accent for the author's own analysis; the only mention of accent is in note 1, reporting that Ousmane Diagana (1980 thesis and 1984 thèse d'Etat on the Soninke of Kaédi, Mauritania) treated Soninke as 'une langue à ton et à accent', an analysis the author explicitly sets aside.

readall_conflicts: One real disagreement. Platiel 1981 (Malian data: her own materials plus the DNAFLA lexicon) holds that Soninke's two-register tone system has lost its distinctive character and that the language carries an intensity accent, one per word, placed by syllable structure (always on the long-vowel syllable of CVVCV, low register; always on the syllable before a geminate in CVCCV, high register; lexically variable and weak in CVCV, absent on the first syllable of CVNCV). Against this, Creissels 2015 (Kingi, Mali) and Y. Diagana 1990 analyse Soninke as a two-tone language with lexical tonal contrasts and never mention stress, and Halaouï 1990 (Mauritania) simply marks tones. Y. Diagana's note 1 records a third position, O. Diagana's (Kaédi, Mauritania, 1980/1984) 'langue à ton et à accent', not opened here. Rialland 1991, which by its title answers Creissels on exactly this prosodic question, could not be opened. Diagana 1985 and both Grégoire articles are silent.

sources.quote: Bakel Soninke data. Ch.6 analyses a tone system: roots carry a tonal plane, non-root morphemes are lexically toneless and get tone by spreading/floating-tone assignment/default H; three purely tonal morphemes (floating L 'complétude' suffix causing downstep or final falling contour; two L boundary prefixes). §6.2: 'Lexicalement le système soninké est à registre marqué bas' with lexical inventory H and L and a surface mid-high tone from downstep. No word stress/accent anywhere (the only 'accent' hit in the text is non-prosodic).

sources.citation: Grégoire, Claire (1987). Morphophonologie et morphologie nominales en soninké. Mandenkan 13. pp. 1-59.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: A segmental morphophonology of nouns (contact rules, nasality, gemination, number and definiteness morphemes) built from published sources (Galtier, the DNAFLA lexicon, the CRES manual, Diagana). Note 1 (p. 5) says the examples are re-transcribed in a phonetic-style graphy showing the result of the contact rules; no tones are marked and neither tone nor accent/stress is mentioned anywhere (the only hits for 'ton' are the French possessive, e.g. 'ton chevreuil', and 'plus haut' = above). scanned of a scan; the search covered every page.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: A morphological study of the perfective/imperfective verb alternation (final-consonant gemination, -nV suffix, vowel loss) based entirely on examples taken from Galtier (1971) and the CRES manual (1977). No tones marked, no mention of tone, accent or stress; the only 'haut' hits are 'plus haut' (above).
